sample.text: men's ODIs between the 12 full members in Cricsheet, 2015-07-05 (current fielding-restriction phases) to 2026-11-18: 828 matches; 695 completed without rain revision and with a full first innings are used for fitting (76 D/L, 32 no result, 25 cut short without a recorded method left out). Cricsheet does not hold every ODI, so this is a sample, not the full record.

claims.claim: Nested shrinkage (year, then ground) gives better ODI first-innings par scores than raw ground averages.
claims.test: Fit par on a random 70% of clean ODIs; predict the first-innings total of the other 30% from the raw ground-year average, the shrunk par, the year average and one global average. Lower RMSE is better.
claims.numbers: RMSE in runs: shrunk 71.63, raw ground-year 77.59, year mean 71.05, global 71.47. Raw minus shrunk, 95% bootstrap interval 0.89 to 11.37. Global minus shrunk -1.86 to 1.23. 91 of 208 test matches were at a ground with no training match that year.
claims.rule: confirmed if the interval for raw minus shrunk is above 0 and shrunk also beats one global average (interval above 0); partly if it only beats the raw averages
claims.our_miss: Most ODI ground-years hold one or two matches, so the raw ground-year average is close to a single score; much of the gain is simply not trusting one match.

claims.claim: The same shrinkage works for par runs in each ODI phase (overs 1-10, 11-40, 41-50).
claims.test: Same held-out test, with the first-innings runs scored in each phase as the target.
claims.numbers: RMSE in runs. overs 1-10: shrunk 14.34, raw 16.25, global 14.19 (raw minus shrunk 1.04 to 2.78; global minus shrunk -0.67 to 0.35); overs 11-40: shrunk 36.64, raw 39.79, global 37.11 (raw minus shrunk 0.2 to 6.55; global minus shrunk -0.27 to 1.31); overs 41-50: shrunk 34.53, raw 39.41, global 34.29 (raw minus shrunk 2.66 to 7.0; global minus shrunk -1.13 to 0.55).
claims.rule: confirmed if, in all three phases, shrunk beats raw and one global average (intervals above 0); partly if it beats raw in at least one phase
claims.our_miss: Phase runs are noisier than totals relative to their spread, and overs 41-50 include innings that were bowled out before over 41 (0 runs).

claims.claim: A DL-style curve (cubic F(w) and beta(w), primer section 4) fits ODI runs-to-come at least as well as the published DL Standard shape, and has the same shape.
claims.test: Fit our curve on first innings of the 70% training ODIs. On the 30% held-out, predict runs still to come at every ball from (a) our curve stretched to the match par, (b) the DL Standard Edition shape (third-party fit to the public table) scaled to the same par. Then compare resource percentages cell by cell.
claims.numbers: Held-out RMSE of runs to come: ours 43.354, DL shape 44.129 (difference in mean squared error, ours minus DL, 95% match bootstrap -139.6 to -10.4). Resource %, ours v DL, at 5 to 40 overs left in states at least 30 first innings passed through: 38 of 42 cells within 5 points; largest gap 5.5 points (15 overs left, 1 down: ours 49.6%, DL 44.1%, 41 innings). At 20 overs left: 0 down ours 63.2% v DL 56.6%; 5 down ours 36.7% v DL 38.6%. R(300,0) = 271.2 runs, beta(0) = 153.3 balls.
claims.rule: confirmed if ours is no worse than the DL shape on held-out data (interval not above 0) and every compared cell (5 to 40 overs left, at least 30 innings) is within 5 percentage points of DL; partly if only one of the two holds
claims.our_miss: The DL Standard values come from a hobbyist fit to the 2000s-era public table, not from the DLS owners; the Professional Edition used in real matches is not published.

claims.claim: High-scoring conditions 'straighten' the curve with an exponent n0 = 1.04 (primer, fitted on T20).
claims.test: Fit n0 on first innings in the top quarter of par, re-solving lambda from par for each candidate; once on all clean ODIs and once on the 70% training split.
claims.numbers: Fitted n0 = 0.001 (all clean ODIs); training-split fit 0.0.
claims.rule: confirmed if fitted n0 is within 0.3 of 1.04; not confirmed if below 0.5 (the fit minimises error, so the fitted value fits at least as well as 1.04); partly otherwise
claims.our_miss: As in T20, a higher par mostly scales the whole curve up; weak evidence either way.

claims.claim: The Pythagorean form r^n / (1 + r^n) with n = 6 (the primer's T20 value) carries over to ODIs.
claims.test: Maximum likelihood for n in each innings on the 70% training ODIs.
claims.numbers: Fitted n = 5.411 (first innings) and 5.814 (chase). With n = 6 on held-out ODIs: ECE 0.039 and 0.0281.
claims.rule: confirmed if both fitted exponents are within 1 of 6
claims.our_miss: The exponent was fitted on ODIs rather than assumed; that it lands near 6 is the finding. Calibration is a separate test (next card).

claims.claim: The method is well calibrated on ODIs it never saw (fitted n plus a Platt shift, as in T20 Lab).
claims.test: Score the 30% held-out ODIs ball by ball; 15 equal-count bins; Brier, ECE, AUC.
claims.numbers: Both innings: Brier 0.1675, ECE 0.0219, AUC 0.8301. First innings ECE 0.0388 (AUC 0.7184); chase ECE 0.0445 (AUC 0.9233).
claims.rule: confirmed if ECE <= 0.03 overall and in each innings; partly if only overall
claims.our_miss: Balls within one match are strongly correlated, so the effective sample is closer to the number of matches than the number of balls.

claims.claim: The curve-based win probability beats a plain baseline (Brier score).
claims.test: Same held-out balls. Baselines: the base rate (no information) and a logistic regression per innings on runs, balls left, wickets, par or runs needed and required rate, fitted on the same 70%.
claims.numbers: Brier, both innings: ours 0.1675, logistic 0.1692, base rate 0.25. Ours minus logistic, 95% match bootstrap -0.0064 to 0.0027; ours minus base rate -0.0983 to -0.0667.
claims.rule: confirmed if ours beats both baselines (intervals below 0); partly if it beats the base rate and is level with the logistic (interval spans 0); not confirmed if the logistic is clearly better
claims.our_miss: The logistic baseline uses the same game-state information; a draw with it means the curve adds interpretability (runs, Impact) rather than accuracy.

claims.claim: Grounds have a lasting effect on ODI first-innings totals, worth estimating with shrinkage (Buffalo Park, East London, as the case).
claims.test: All clean full-member ODIs since 2002: totals relative to that year's average; venue means shrunk with k = within / between variance. Held-out: predict 30% of totals from the year mean alone, or the year mean plus the shrunk venue effect.
claims.numbers: Held-out RMSE: year only 64.86, year + shrunk venue 64.12, year + raw venue 67.44 (year only minus shrunk venue, 95% interval -0.35 to 1.91). k = 5.54 matches. Buffalo Park: 7 matches, raw effect 0.7 runs, shrunk 0.4 runs (weight 0.558).
claims.n: 1731 matches at 144 venues (1212 train / 519 test; this test uses every era since 2002, not only the 2015 sample); Buffalo Park n = 7 (small)
claims.rule: confirmed if the interval for year-only minus year+venue RMSE is above 0; partly if the point estimate is above 0 but the interval spans 0; not confirmed otherwise
claims.our_miss: Buffalo Park's 7 matches span many years and pitches; its shrunk effect is an estimate with a wide margin, not a fact about the 2026 pitch.

misses: Calibration by innings missed our own 0.03 target after the fitted shift (ECE 0.0388 first innings, 0.0445 chase): the shift fitted on training ODIs did not carry cleanly to the test set. For the chase the plain n = 6 form did better (ECE 0.0281).

Our curve-based win probability is level with a plain logistic regression on the same scoreboard (Brier 0.1675 v 0.1692, interval of the difference -0.0064 to 0.0027): it adds runs-based readings such as Impact, not accuracy.
For first-innings totals, shrunk par does no better than one average for the year (RMSE 71.63 v 71.05): most ODI grounds host one or two matches a year.
The straightening exponent n0 fitted at 0.001, as in T20: in our data a higher par scales the curve rather than reshaping it.
Cricsheet does not hold every ODI, rain-revised matches are left out of fitting, and the DL comparison uses a third-party fit to the public Standard Edition table, not the Professional Edition.
The South Africa and Bangladesh tables are descriptive: small samples, different opponents and grounds, no adjustment for opposition strength.
